newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's ruling party loses grip on key state.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's ruling party loses grip on key state.

text.p: A Mexican election tribunal has stripped the ruling party of its legislative majority in the key central State of Mexico after recent elections there, state officials said on Tuesday.

The move reverses an earlier decision by a state electoral council that gave eight additional seats in the local congress to the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) following Nov. 10 state elections.

The eight seats were supposed to have been divided up proportionally among the opposition parties, according to Mexican electoral law. Had they remained in PRI hands, the party would have had a majority in the state legislature.
But the state's highest electoral body decided late on Monday that the earlier decision was illegal -- and divided up the eight seats among the opposition.
The PRI would have had 38 seats compared to 37 seats for the opposition under the previous ruling, but it will now have 30 of 75 seats -- well short of an absolute majority.
The State of Mexico is the country's most populous state, with more than 11 million residents. It is also a major industrial state and practically surrounds the capital city.
Opposition politicians welcomed the decision and said it restored some credibility to pledges by President Ernesto Zedillo to run a country that holds clean elections.
"The PRI's monolithic control over politics in this state has ended," Jose Gutierrez, the state leader of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution, told reporters on Tuesday.
